questions.text: Why did Lencho call the raindrops 'new coins' and the hailstones 'new silver coins'? What does it show about him? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Lencho was a poor farmer who depended wholly on his crop. For him rain meant money, so big raindrops looked like ten-centavo coins and hailstones like five-centavo silver pieces. It shows his hope, his simplicity and his dependence on the harvest.

questions.text: Describe the destruction caused by the hailstorm in Lencho's field. (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The rain turned into a hailstorm which beat down on the house, the corn and the beans. The field was covered with white as if with salt. Not a leaf remained on the trees, the corn was destroyed and the flowers were gone from the plants.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Why did the postmaster decide to answer Lencho's letter? How did he manage to do so? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The postmaster was moved by Lencho's unshakeable faith in God and did not want to destroy it. He collected money from his employees, gave part of his own salary and friends contributed, and finally sent Lencho seventy pesos, signing the letter 'God'.

questions.text: Why was Lencho angry when he counted the money in the envelope? Whom did he blame? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Lencho had asked for a hundred pesos but found only seventy. Since he was sure God could never make a mistake, he thought the post-office employees had kept the rest, and called them a bunch of crooks.

questions.text: 'Lencho's faith in God was unshakeable.' Support this statement with two examples from the lesson. (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Lencho prayed on seeing the hailstorm's destruction and wrote a letter addressed directly to God, asking for a hundred pesos. When he received only seventy, he did not doubt God but suspected the postal staff. Both show his deep faith.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What was the postmaster's first reaction on seeing the address on Lencho's letter, and how did it change? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The postmaster burst out laughing at a letter addressed to God. But on reading it, he became serious and was filled with admiration for Lencho's faith. He felt he should reply so that the farmer's faith would not be shaken.

questions.text: 'The postmaster and Lencho are both men of faith, yet they differ.' Compare the two characters with reference to 'A Letter to God'. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: Lencho, a hard-working farmer, has simple, complete faith in God and trusts that He will meet his need. The postmaster, a fat, amiable man, has faith in humanity and goodness. He laughs at first but then, moved by the letter, decides to help, collecting money from his staff and adding from his own salary. Lencho's faith is blind: he calls the post-office employees crooks when he finds less money. The postmaster is practical, kind and compassionate and prefers to keep the farmer's belief alive. Lencho teaches the value of faith, but the postmaster shows that sometimes God's help comes through human beings. Together they show that faith and kindness are both essential, and that human goodness can silently answer prayers.

questions.text: What does Mandela say about the two anthems sung at the inauguration, and why was this significant? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Two national anthems were sung: 'Die Stem', earlier the anthem of the whites, and 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika', the anthem of the blacks. Earlier each side disliked the other's anthem, so singing both showed the nation was being united.

questions.text: What did Mandela mean by saying 'the brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear'? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Mandela felt fear many times, especially in prison, but he learned that courage is not the absence of fear. A brave person feels fear yet does not let it stop him; he overcomes it and does what is right.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: How does Mandela describe the system of apartheid that had existed in South Africa? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Mandela describes apartheid as an unjust system in which one group oppressed another because of colour. It created a deep and lasting wound in the country and divided people by race. The new government was to end it forever.

questions.text: Mandela said that he was only the sum of all those African patriots who had gone before him. What did he mean? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Mandela did not claim credit alone for the victory. He said the freedom struggle had been carried on for generations by many brave men and women, and his own success rested on their sacrifices; he only represented them.

questions.text: Who were the dignitaries present at the inauguration, and how did the military show its allegiance to the new government? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Dignitaries from more than a hundred and forty countries attended, the largest gathering of international leaders on South African soil. The country's military generals, once opposed to him, saluted him and pledged loyalty to the new government.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What two kinds of freedom did Mandela speak about, and what did he finally realise? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: As a boy he thought of freedom as the 'obvious' kind, to run in the fields and swim in the stream. Later he realised that it was the freedom of his whole people that mattered, and that a free life must respect and enhance the freedom of others.

questions.text: How does Mandela describe the ceremony of the inauguration, and what does it reveal about the new South Africa? (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: The ceremony took place in an amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria on a bright autumn day. Thousands of people, black and white, and leaders from many countries attended. Military generals saluted him, jets flew overhead and two national anthems were sung. For Mandela the day was a victory over the system of racial discrimination that had existed for decades. He took the oath and declared that never again would one people oppress another. He remembered the sacrifices of countless freedom fighters. The picture is of a rainbow nation, united, in which freedom and justice were new in the country's history, and Mandela's thoughts on courage and freedom bring out the lesson of the whole struggle.

questions.text: 'The oppressor must be liberated just as surely as the oppressed.' Explain this idea with reference to the lesson. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: Mandela believed that a man who takes away another man's freedom is a prisoner of hatred, locked behind bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness. The oppressor and the oppressed are both robbed of their humanity. Apartheid made whites afraid and blacks helpless, so both needed freedom. Mandela said that freedom is not merely casting off one's chains but living in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others. This is why, after his release, he did not seek revenge but worked for reconciliation. He saw that the real task of the new government was to create a society in which all people, whatever their colour, could live as equals in dignity and with mutual respect.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly? How did his parents try to encourage him? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The young seagull was afraid because he had never tried and feared he would fall into the sea. His family flew and begged him; his mother tempted him by holding a piece of fish just out of his reach, hoping hunger would make him fly.

questions.text: How did the young seagull finally manage to fly? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The seagull, hungry and driven by desperation, dived at the fish held by his mother and fell off the ledge. To his surprise his wings opened and he found he could fly. His fear vanished once he took the risk.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What happened to the narrator's aeroplane in 'The Black Aeroplane'? How did he get out of difficulty? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The narrator's old Dakota ran into a thick storm with little fuel left and he was lost in cloud. Suddenly he saw a black aeroplane with no lights. He followed it, and it guided him until he saw the airfield below and landed safely.

questions.text: Why did the controller express surprise when the pilot said he had followed another aeroplane? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The controller told the pilot that there was no other aeroplane in the sky that night and that he had been flying alone. This made the pilot realise that the black plane had been a mysterious helper which saved him in the storm.

questions.text: Compare the fear experienced by the seagull and the narrator pilot. (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The seagull feared falling into the sea while the pilot feared being lost in a storm. Both overcame their fear: the seagull by taking a daring leap, and the pilot by trusting the unknown aeroplane and keeping calm.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Why did Anne Frank decide to write a diary and call it 'Kitty'? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Anne had no real friend to confide in. She felt that paper had more patience than people, so she began a diary to share her feelings and called it Kitty, treating it as a friend who would listen to her.

questions.text: How did Anne get out of trouble with Mr Keesing for talking too much? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Mr Keesing gave her extra work, an essay on 'A Chatterbox'. Anne wrote it cleverly, and when he gave a further essay, she wrote a rhyme about ducks with a friend's help. It made him laugh and he ended the punishment.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What restrictions were put on Jews during that period according to the diary? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Jews had to wear a yellow star, were not allowed to ride trams or drive cars, could shop only between 3 and 5 pm, and had to go to Jewish schools. They were forbidden from many public places, which made Anne feel confined.

questions.text: What does Anne's diary reveal about her character? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Anne was lively, talkative, witty and intelligent. She was honest in her thoughts, sensitive about her loneliness and brave even when under fear. She could laugh at herself, as shown by her handling of Mr Keesing.

questions.text: Why does Anne consider her diary a better confidant than a human friend? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Anne felt that people might not understand or might repeat her secrets, whereas a diary would patiently keep all that she felt. She could say anything without being judged, which is why she valued it.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: How did Mr Keesing's attitude towards Anne change? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: At first he was annoyed at her chatter and punished her. But Anne's humorous writings made him laugh and he gave up. In the end he took it in good humour and let her talk, so their relationship grew friendly.

questions.text: 'Anne Frank was a remarkable girl despite the dark times.' Justify with reference to the diary entries. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: Anne lived in the shadow of the Nazi persecution of Jews, yet her diary shows a young girl with courage and humour. She admitted she was lonely and had no friend to confide in, so she created Kitty. She dealt with her teacher Mr Keesing's punishments with wit, writing a clever essay and a rhyme to turn his anger into laughter. She could observe, analyse and laugh at herself and the world. Her thoughts on the restrictions imposed on Jews show maturity. She did not complain but wrote down her feelings truthfully. Her optimism, intelligence and need to share her feelings make her an inspiring figure whose diary has become a record of the human spirit against oppression.

questions.text: Why are the Goan bakers still an important part of Goan life, according to 'Glimpses of India'? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Bread is a part of Goan daily and festive life. The baker, who comes with his bamboo and jingling sound, delivers loaves at the door. Bread is needed in marriages, feasts and celebrations, so the baker holds an important place even today.

questions.text: Describe the baker's typical appearance and dress in Goa. (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The baker wore a kind of long frock, a kabai, which reached down to the knees. This was a relic of the Portuguese days. He moved from door to door with a basket on his head and a bamboo, announcing his arrival.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What makes the people of Coorg unique? Why do they think they are of Greek or Arab descent? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Coorgis are brave and proud, and have a martial tradition. They are said to be of Greek or Arab origin since some believe a few of Alexander's soldiers settled there, and their long black coat with an embroidered waistband resembles Arab dress.

questions.text: Which Coorgi soldiers are mentioned as the pride of India? What does this show about the people of Coorg? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: General Cariappa and General Thimayya are mentioned, who led the Indian army. They belonged to Coorg. It shows that Coorg people have a strong martial spirit and a long tradition of serving the nation with courage.

questions.text: Why was Rajvir interested in Pranjol's remarks about the tea plant? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Pranjol Barua was an Assamese tea planter's son who explained how tea was grown. His talk of the estate and of the plant's discovery fascinated Rajvir, who had never seen the tea-making process and was eager to learn about it.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Describe the natural beauty of Coorg and the character of its people as presented in 'Glimpses of India'. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: Coorg is a lovely hilly district in Karnataka, the land of the Kodavus. It is a land of misty hills, green forests, coffee plantations and the sources of river Kaveri. The weather is pleasant and the scenery inspires travellers. The people are well known for their hospitality, courage and martial pride; they love hunting and dance and are free to carry weapons without a licence. The Coorg Regiment is one of the most decorated in the Indian army. Their fiery temperament is balanced by kindness towards guests. Thus Coorg is a beautiful and proud land where nature and the brave people together make visitors feel at home.

questions.text: How did Gavin Maxwell get his pet otter, and how did he name it? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Maxwell, while living in Iraq, was given an otter by his friend Wilfred Thesiger, who found it in the marshes of the Tigris. Maxwell named it Mijbil and took it with him to London as a pet.

questions.text: How did Mijbil behave during the journey to London? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Mijbil was put in a box with holes. During the flight he escaped from the box, and clambered over passengers, causing panic. Maxwell managed to catch him. In general, the otter was restless but he calmed after being petted.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: How did Mijbil react to water in the bathroom? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Mijbil was delighted with water. When the tap was turned on, he leapt into the tub and rolled and splashed around in joy. Water seemed to be as natural for him as air for humans, and he flooded the place with his excited play.

questions.text: What did Mijbil's play with the rubber ball show about him? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Mijbil loved to play with a ball. He tossed it, chased it, and held it by his claws. It showed that he was playful, intelligent and had a strong sense of fun and curiosity, like a human child.

questions.text: Why did Maxwell call Mijbil a 'creature of moods'? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The otter's mood changed quickly. At times he was playful and affectionate, at other times restless and nervous in strange places. Maxwell understood that an otter must be handled with patience and understanding, as its behaviour followed its feelings.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What does the lesson tell us about the author's attitude towards animals? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Maxwell loved animals and studied them carefully. He treated Mijbil like a family member, with patience and affection, and was ready to take trouble for his comfort. The lesson shows his respect for the animal's nature.

questions.text: Describe Mijbil's first days with the author and show how the author coped with an unusual pet. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: Maxwell took the otter home in a box and let him out in the room. At first Mijbil was nervous, but he soon became friendly and was curious about everything. His love for water was shown when he played in the bath and made a mess. The author provided a ball with which Mijbil played endlessly. Though the otter could be mischievous, Maxwell remained patient and affectionate. He understood the animal's needs: water, play and company. His care built trust, and the otter became a loving pet. The lesson shows that kindness and patience can build friendship between humans and animals.

questions.text: Why was Valli fascinated by the bus? What was her wish? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Valli was a curious eight-year-old girl who lived in a village. The bus passed by her house every day and she longed to ride it and see the town and the world beyond her street.

questions.text: How did Valli get money for the bus ride? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Valli did not ask her mother for the money. She saved the coins she got, which she managed to collect after a lot of difficult work and waiting, and kept them safe until she felt there was enough to ride to the town and back.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: How did the conductor behave when Valli boarded the bus? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The conductor was surprised to see a small girl travelling alone. He teased her calling her 'Madam' and asked her to pay the fare. Valli, proud of being called madam, behaved like a grown-up passenger.

questions.text: What did Valli see on her way that disturbed her? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: On her way Valli saw a dead cow on the road, a sight that frightened and saddened her. It made her aware for the first time that the world also had ugly, sad things apart from the beautiful things she had imagined.

questions.text: How did Valli try to show that she was a grown-up passenger during the journey? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Valli was proud and wished to be treated as a grown-up, independent 'madam'. She sat by the window, behaved seriously and paid her own fare, and did not like to be treated as a small child.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What is the central idea of 'Madam Rides the Bus'? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The lesson shows a child's journey from innocence to experience. Valli's dream of the bus ride is fulfilled but she also meets the harsh realities of life such as death. It shows growing up and a sense of independence.

questions.text: How does the writer use humour in the story? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The writer smiles at Valli's pride when she is addressed as 'madam' and at her serious air as a passenger, though she is a child. The contrast between her tiny size and her grown-up manners creates gentle humour.

questions.text: 'Valli's first journey brought her both joy and a lesson about life.' Elaborate. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: Valli's journey was the fulfilment of a long dream. She had saved up money and secretly boarded the bus. She felt grown-up when the conductor called her 'madam'. She enjoyed the view outside the window, the trees, fields and people. Her curiosity and confidence made her feel like a free person. But the journey also had its darker side. On the way she saw the dead body of a cow and was deeply disturbed. She realised that life is not only about beauty and enjoyment, but also about suffering and death. Valli's pride and innocence gave way to a sober understanding. The story shows how a child's first adventure becomes a step in growing up.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Why did Lomov visit Chubukov's house in formal dress? What was his purpose? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Lomov came in a dress coat and white gloves because he came to propose marriage to Natalya, Chubukov's daughter. Chubukov at first thought he had come to borrow money, but Lomov explained that he wanted to ask for Natalya's hand.

questions.text: What ailments did Lomov suffer from, and how did they affect the proposal? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Lomov suffered from palpitations, twitching of the eyelid and numbness in the legs, which got worse whenever he was excited. They made him anxious, and during the quarrels his nerves gave way and he fainted, delaying the proposal.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What was the quarrel over 'Oxen Meadows'? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Lomov said the Oxen Meadows were his, while Natalya insisted they belonged to her family. Both argued about who had the legal ownership. The quarrel grew bitter and spoilt the mood of proposing marriage.

questions.text: How does Chubukov change his behaviour once he learns Lomov's purpose? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: At first he spoke politely, then he was delighted and called Lomov 'my darling' and 'my angel'. Later he turned hostile when Lomov quarrelled over the meadows, and finally pushed the two to marry.

questions.text: Why does the play end with the characters quarrelling again? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: After the engagement, Lomov and Natalya began quarrelling over the merits of their dogs. This shows that both were quarrelsome by nature and the marriage would perhaps be full of arguments, creating a humorous ending.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: How does the playwright satirise the Russian landowners in 'The Proposal'? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Anton Chekhov shows landowners who are interested in property, status and trivial matters rather than love. Their quarrels over land and dogs show their greed and pride, making the proposal a farce.

questions.text: 'The Proposal' is a farce on human nature. Explain. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: In 'The Proposal', a simple marriage proposal turns into a series of quarrels. Lomov, nervous and a hypochondriac, and Natalya, strong-willed and proud, argue over the ownership of the Oxen Meadows and the merits of their dogs Squeezer and Guess. Chubukov, who is keen to see his daughter married, joins the quarrel and says harsh things to Lomov. When Lomov faints, Chubukov thinks he has died and laments. Natalya, once she realises Lomov's intention, calls him back. Then, when they are engaged, they begin to argue again. The play uses exaggeration and comic situations to show how petty and quarrelsome people can be. It also shows that human beings often lose sight of what is important because of vanity and pride.

questions.text: Who was Kisa Gotami and why did she go to the Buddha? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Kisa Gotami was a young woman whose only son died. Overcome by grief, she carried the dead child from house to house asking for medicine. A kind man advised her to go to the Buddha, who alone could help her.

questions.text: What did the Buddha ask Kisa Gotami to bring for the medicine? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The Buddha asked her to bring a handful of mustard seed from a house where no one had ever lost a child, husband, parent or friend. This was his way of teaching her that death comes to every family.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Why could Kisa Gotami not get the mustard seed? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: She went from house to house, and though people were ready to give the seed, they said that the living were few and the dead were many; every family had lost someone. She understood that she was not the only one who suffered.

questions.text: How did Kisa Gotami's attitude change after her search for mustard seed? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: She stopped being selfish in her grief and realised that death is the law of all living beings. She buried the child, came back calm and became a follower of the Buddha, who had made her see the truth gently.

questions.text: What did the Buddha mean when he said that 'the life of mortals in this world is troubled and brief and combined with pain'? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The Buddha taught that human life is short, full of troubles and sorrows, and that no one can escape death. He wished Kisa Gotami to see that grief is universal and one must accept it with calm.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: 'The Buddha did not directly tell Kisa Gotami that her son could not be revived.' Why do you think he chose an indirect way? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: A grieving mother in shock might not have accepted a plain statement. By asking her to find mustard seed, the Buddha let her discover the truth by herself, which was more convincing and less painful for her.

questions.text: What does the lesson teach us about dealing with grief? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The lesson teaches that grief is shared by all, that death is natural and unavoidable, and that we should accept it with courage. We should not give way to sorrow but help others and continue to live wisely.

questions.text: How did the people of the town respond to Kisa Gotami's request for medicine? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Some people pitied her and thought she had lost her senses. They told her that her child was dead and no medicine would help. One wise man, however, told her to approach the Buddha, who could help her.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Describe in your own words how the Buddha helped Kisa Gotami overcome her grief. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: Kisa Gotami's son had died and in her sorrow she carried him asking people for medicine. Some mocked her, but a wise man sent her to the Buddha. The Buddha did not say that her son was dead and gone; he asked her to bring a handful of mustard seed from a house where no one had died. Hopeful, Kisa Gotami went from door to door but found that every house had known death. She came to realise that she was not alone in her suffering. This made her understand the truth about the nature of life and death. She took the child to the forest, buried him and returned to the Buddha, calm and wiser. The Buddha's method shows that true wisdom lies in letting a person see the truth for herself.

questions.text: 'The Sermon at Benares' tells us how to overcome sorrow. What message does the Buddha give to humankind? (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: The Buddha says that life is short, troubled and mixed with pain, and that death comes to all. No one can avoid it, and lamenting does not bring back the dead. Weeping only increases pain and harms the body. He asks people to draw out the arrow of grief and be calm. Through the story of Kisa Gotami he shows that everyone must suffer loss and that sharing this truth makes the burden lighter. The wise do not grieve but accept the law of the world. The message is to face death with peace, wisdom and compassion for others.

questions.text: Why did Mrs Pumphrey bring Tricki Woo to Siegfried's surgery, and what was the diagnosis? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Tricki Woo was a Pekinese dog who was lazy, overfed and became sick. Mrs Pumphrey, his doting owner, brought him as he seemed unwell. Siegfried found that Tricki was suffering from over-eating and lack of exercise.

questions.text: How did Herriot cure Tricki Woo? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Herriot kept Tricki in the surgery, put him on a strict diet and gave him exercise with other dogs. Tricki began to play with the dogs, and was soon cured of his over-eating and became fit and active.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Why did Mrs Pumphrey send gifts to the surgery during Tricki's stay? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Mrs Pumphrey missed Tricki and worried about him. She sent hampers, eggs, wine and other things, thinking Tricki needed them. It shows her excessive love for her pet, which almost proved harmful.

questions.text: What is the irony in the title 'A Triumph of Surgery'? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: There was no real surgery. Tricki was merely overfed, and cured by diet and exercise. Mrs Pumphrey calls it a triumph of surgery, thinking Herriot had performed a miracle. The title is thus humorous and ironic.

questions.text: How does the lesson point to the dangers of too much pampering? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Mrs Pumphrey's constant feeding and pampering made Tricki Woo ill. Only when he was kept away from her indulgence, and made to eat less and exercise, did he recover, showing that excessive care can harm.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Who was Hari Singh? How did he become a thief? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Hari Singh was a fifteen-year-old boy who earned his living as a thief. He was clever at cheating and stealing and had taken to it from childhood. Poverty and the lack of anyone to guide him pushed him into it.

questions.text: How did Anil treat Hari Singh when they first met? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Anil, a young writer, was kind and trusting. He gave Hari a job as a cook, offered him food and a place to stay, and promised to teach him to read and write, though he knew Hari was a thief.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Why did Hari Singh plan to rob Anil? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Hari had come to Anil only to rob him. When Anil, a writer, received a sum of money, Hari saw his chance. His plan was to wait for it, take the notes and run away.

questions.text: What did Anil's trust do to Hari Singh? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Anil's trust and kindness made Hari uncomfortable. He had never been treated with such faith. This confused him and slowly began to change his thinking; he felt guilty about betraying the one person who cared for him.

questions.text: What lesson does 'The Thief's Story' teach us? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The story teaches that trust and kindness can reform a person. Anil's affection and faith in Hari work better than punishment, and show that even a thief has a conscience which can be awakened.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Who is Ausable? What does his conversation with Fowler reveal about him? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Ausable is a secret agent who pretends to be an ordinary man in a hotel room. He is calm, clever and humorous. His easy talk with Fowler hides his alertness and his skill in handling dangerous visitors.

questions.text: Why did Ausable make a show of complaining about the balcony, and what was the truth? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Ausable complained loudly about a nuisance of a balcony as part of a clever act to deceive the intruder. In fact his room had no balcony at all. His acting showed his skill and calm.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: Why was Fowler surprised at Ausable's behaviour? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Fowler, a young writer who had come to interview Ausable, was amazed that Ausable remained calm when an armed intruder entered. He wondered how a secret agent could think quickly and stay so composed.

questions.text: How does Ausable's way of handling the dangerous visitor show his courage? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Ausable did not panic when faced with danger. He stayed calm, spoke lightly and used his quick thinking and acting to outwit the intruder. His courage lay in his coolness and presence of mind, not in force.

questions.text: What is the importance of presence of mind as shown in the story? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The story shows that presence of mind can save one's life. Ausable stayed cool and used his wit to defeat an armed enemy. A clever mind is more powerful than force.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: How does the story end, and what makes it a twist? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The ending reveals that Ausable was in fact a secret agent and Fowler a writer was unaware. The unexpected facts, such as the non-existent balcony, surprise the reader and give the story a clever twist.

questions.text: Who was Horace Danby? How did he spend his life? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Horace Danby was a respected, hard-working lock-maker. He lived a quiet life and loved rare books. Once a year he secretly committed a robbery to raise money to buy books, and otherwise appeared honest.

questions.text: Why did Horace decide to commit a robbery once a year? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: He loved rare books, which were costly. To collect money for them he planned one robbery every year in the house of a rich person, while living an honest life otherwise.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What precautions did Horace take before the robbery? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: He studied the house and found out that the owner was out, wore gloves so as not to leave fingerprints, and brought tools. He was a careful man who planned every step beforehand.

questions.text: What happened when the woman appeared in the house? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: A woman appeared and spoke politely to Horace, claiming to be the owner. She asked him to open the safe, and he obeyed without suspicion. She was in fact another thief.

questions.text: How did Horace's trust in the woman backfire? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Horace took off his gloves and opened the safe, leaving his fingerprints. The woman took the jewels and left. Later the police traced him through his fingerprints and arrested him.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What does the title 'A Question of Trust' mean? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The title points to Horace's misplaced trust in the woman and the way trust is used by cheats. Horace trusts a stranger and is deceived. It raises the question of whom to trust and whether a thief can trust another.

questions.text: What irony do we see in the ending of the story? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Horace, a thief, was tricked by another thief, and suffered for her crime. The man who planned carefully was undone by an unplanned act of trust. This irony makes the story amusing and shows that crime does not pay.

questions.text: What is the humour in the end of the story? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Horace was sent to prison for the crime. The ending is humorous: a man who robbed to buy books ended up in prison, away from his beloved books. It shows that crime does not pay.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: 'Horace Danby was a thief but a likeable one.' Do you agree? Support your answer with reference to the story. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: Horace Danby was a respectable lock-maker who loved books and led a simple life. He committed only one robbery in a year, only to buy rare books. He did not harm anyone and was kind and shy. This makes the reader like him. He planned carefully and wore gloves, but his helpfulness made him trust a stranger, a woman who tricked him. He was caught by the police because he left fingerprints. His mistake was not malice but misplaced trust. While one cannot approve his dishonesty, his weakness for books, his gentle manners and the comic outcome make him a character the reader sympathises with. The story shows that even a decent person can be led into wrongdoing and be punished.

questions.text: Describe the sequence of events in the house Horace Danby robbed in 'A Question of Trust'. (Answer in about 100-120 words.)
questions.answer: Horace Danby went to the house when the owner was away. He entered, took out his tools and began on the safe, having removed his gloves. A woman appeared and, claiming to be the owner, asked him to carry on. Trusting her, Horace opened the safe and she took the jewels. Horace's fingerprints were left at the scene and the police traced and arrested him. The events show how a clever woman beat a man who was too trusting.

questions.text: Who is Griffin? How did he become invisible? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Griffin was a scientist who made a discovery that made him invisible. He experimented with chemicals and managed to make himself invisible, but was cold and hungry when he went out, as he could not wear any clothes.

questions.text: Why did Griffin find invisibility a disadvantage? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Griffin found that he could not wear clothes, which made him feel cold. Footprints could be seen in the snow, people bumped into him and he could not eat in public. The gift turned into a burden.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: How did Griffin try to hide his invisibility from people? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: He covered himself with clothes, a hat, bandages and spectacles and a false nose. This helped him look like a normal person, though people were curious about his strange appearance.

questions.text: What does the title 'Footprints Without Feet' signify? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The title refers to the footprints that appear in the snow although the person who made them cannot be seen. It points to the mystery of the invisible man, and also to the one clue through which he can be traced.

questions.text: What qualities of Griffin are shown in the story? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: Griffin is shown as clever, ambitious and determined as a scientist. But he is also selfish, rude and impatient. His wish for personal gain makes him a lonely and troubled figure.
questions.basis: variant of sample-paper literature question on this lesson

questions.text: What lesson can we learn from the story of Griffin? (Answer in about 40-50 words.)
questions.answer: The story teaches that scientific discovery used selfishly can bring trouble. Griffin's ability brought him loneliness and fear instead of happiness. Knowledge must be used with responsibility and care for others.

questions.text:
Read the passage given below.

1. Every morning, in the narrow lanes of old Varanasi, a small group of boys gathers around a tea-stall owner named Raghunath. He is not a teacher, yet the boys, who sell flowers and newspapers to tourists, come to him with their books. Raghunath left school after class five, because his family could not afford the fees, and he has regretted it all his life. Seven years ago, he decided that no child near his stall would miss out on learning if he could help it.

2. It began quite simply. A young flower seller named Imran asked him to read a letter that had come from his uncle. Raghunath, who had taught himself to read from old newspapers, did it gladly. Soon Imran's friends asked him to help with sums, and by the end of the month, six children were sitting on the wooden bench outside the stall, working through their notebooks after the morning rush.

3. Raghunath has no money to spare, so he improvises. A discarded bedsheet, painted black, serves as a board. Customers who stay for a second cup of tea often leave behind their old newspapers, which become reading material. A retired bank clerk visits twice a week to teach arithmetic, and a college student comes on Sundays to teach English. None of them is paid.

4. The results have surprised many people. Three of Raghunath's students have been admitted to the local government school, and one has won a small scholarship. Some of the shopkeepers nearby have also started donating pencils and notebooks. 'I only provide a bench and a little time,' Raghunath says with a smile. 'The children bring the hunger to learn. That is the real fuel.'

questions.text:
Read the passage given below.

1. The Sundarbans, spread across India and Bangladesh, form the largest mangrove forest in the world. The region is a maze of rivers, creeks and tiny islands that are flooded twice a day by the tides. It is home to the famous Royal Bengal Tiger, which has learnt to swim across the salty channels in search of prey.

2. Mangrove trees are remarkable survivors. Their roots rise above the muddy ground like thin pegs, helping them to breathe in soil that has very little oxygen. These dense roots also hold the soil together and slow down the waves, acting as a natural wall against storms and cyclones. When a severe cyclone hit the region some years ago, villages protected by thick mangroves suffered far less damage than those without them.

3. Despite their value, the mangroves face serious threats. Rising sea levels are making the water more salty, and some islands are slowly sinking. Clearing of forest for farming and shrimp ponds has reduced the area under trees. Many villagers who depend on the forest for honey, fish and crabs are forced to take risks, entering the jungle where tigers roam.

4. Efforts to protect the Sundarbans are now under way. Local women's groups have begun planting mangrove saplings along the embankments, and the forest department has set up fenced areas to keep tigers away from villages. Schools hold awareness programmes, teaching children that the forest is not an obstacle to progress but the very shield that protects their homes.

5. Scientists say that saving the Sundarbans is not just a local matter. Mangroves store more carbon than many other forests, which makes them valuable in fighting climate change. If the world values them, the beautiful forest may continue to guard both its people and the planet.
